chapter_theme: The worth of speech about the limitless (வரையுரை மாட்சி): once one has lost one's limits and become the Lord, there is nothing left to bound, think of or choose; those who talk of the unspeakable are mutes, while the Lord is plain to a mind as clear as still water, and the truth is to rest in examining oneself once the mind's maya dies.
structure_note: Three verses: questions to those who would describe the state (2954), the mutes who talk of it against the still mind (2955), and the mind's maya, whose ending is the truth (2956). The title's sense is uncertain: வரை can be limit, and also choosing in marriage.

2954.reading: Once one's own limits are gone, whom is there to limit? Once one has become He, whom is there to think of? Whom does the eye that conquered Kama favour? Tell me that word, you of pure speech.
2954.nuance: வரைவு is limit or bounding, and in love poetry also the choosing of a bride, so the first line may also ask 'whom is there to wed?' The eye that conquered Kama is Siva's third eye, which burned the god of love, or the jnani's eye that has mastered desire. The closing line is likely ironic, addressed to those who think the state can be spoken.

2955.reading: You mutes who speak of the one that is beyond speech, can the shore of what has no shore be seen? To those whose thought grows clear like water without waves, the one with twisted matted hair stays without any veil.
2955.nuance: The talkers are called mutes because their words reach nothing. புரையற்று can mean without fault or without any hiding place; with the image of clear, still water, being seen plainly fits better.

2956.reading: The mind's maya is maya, and this maya is delusion; when the mind's maya itself dies there is nothing else, nothing dies after that, and no need to babble: to remain having examined oneself is the truth.
2956.nuance: தத்துவம் here likely means the real or the truth rather than one of the thirty-six tattvas, though the technical sense may also be heard. பிதற்றவும் வேண்டா echoes the previous verse's mutes.

links.note: Both use muteness against false silence: in 1896 one whose speech alone stops is merely mute (மூங்கை) while true silence stills the mind too; here those who talk of the unspeakable are the mutes, and the Lord is seen by the mind gone still.
